query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating the AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with a sub-micron oxide dispersion (e.g., Y2O3 nanoparticles) and processing it via a low-thermal-input laser powder bed fusion regime will reduce residual thermal stresses and improve mechanical properties by promoting heterogeneous nucleation and refined microstructure, compared to components produced under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock in its as-received state without nanoparticle modification.
generation.intervention: Introduce a nanoparticle dispersion coating onto the AlCrFeNiSi powder (using, e.g., resonant acoustic mixing to uniformly disperse Y2O3 nanoparticles) and process the modified powder using a lowered laser power with increased scanning speed in L-PBF.
generation.conditions: Applicable for miniature components (<1 cm scale) manufactured in an inert (argon) atmosphere with a layer thickness of approximately 20–40 µm and using a low-thermal-load processing window (e.g., laser power reduced by ~25–40% relative to conventional settings, with tailored hatch spacing to ensure sufficient overlapping of melt pools).
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formed nanoscale oxide precipitates act as heterogeneous nucleation sites, promoting grain refinement and a more uniform microstructure while also enhancing thermal conductivity to mitigate steep thermal gradients.
generation.mechanism: The oxide nanoparticles lower the energy barrier for nucleation during solidification, thereby refining the grain structure and reducing the build-up of residual thermal stresses. This improved microstructure mediates mechanical properties by enhancing strength and ductility, while the lower thermal input simplifies process control by minimizing high thermal gradients.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed components, the modified components are expected to exhibit lower residual stresses (detectable via X-ray diffraction stress mapping), finer and more uniform grain sizes (observable via SEM/TEM), and improved mechanical performance such as higher yield strength with maintained ductility.
generation.baseline: Conventional high-thermal-load AM processing of AlCrFeNiSi powder, which typically results in high residual stresses and degraded mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is most applicable to miniature components produced via L-PBF under controlled, low-energy input conditions; results may vary for larger geometries or processing conditions outside the specified window.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal nanoparticle concentration, exact laser processing parameters, and the generality of the intervention across different AM systems remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components via laser powder bed fusion: one using the standard (high thermal load) processing and the other using the nanoparticle-coated powder with the low-thermal-input processing parameters. Ensure all other parameters are held constant. Post-process both sets identically.
measurements: Residual stress measurement using X-ray diffraction mapping.
Microstructural characterization via SEM/TEM to assess grain size and distribution of precipitates.
Mechanical testing (tensile/compression tests) to quantify yield strength, ductility, and overall performance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticle-coated, low-thermal-input processed components do not show statistically significant reductions in residual stress, grain refinement, and improvement in mechanical properties compared to the conventional components, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Material-agnostic machine learning approach enables high relative density in powder bed fusion products

Abstract: This study introduces a method that is applicable across various powder materials to predict process conditions that yield a product with a relative density greater than 98% by laser powder bed fusion. We develop an XGBoost model using a dataset comprising material properties of powder and process conditions, and its output, relative density, undergoes a transformation using a sigmoid function to increase accuracy. We deeply examine the relationships between input features and the target value using Shapley additive explanations. Experimental validation with stainless steel 316 L, AlSi10Mg, and Fe60Co15Ni15Cr10 medium entropy alloy powders verifies the method’s reproducibility and transferability. This research contributes to laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing by offering a universally applicable strategy to optimize process conditions. Additive manufacturing of alloys with programmable microstructure and properties

Abstract: AbstractIn metallurgy, mechanical deformation is essential to engineer the microstructure of metals and to tailor their mechanical properties. However, this practice is inapplicable to near-net-shape metal parts produced by additive manufacturing (AM), since it would irremediably compromise their carefully designed geometries. In this work, we show how to circumvent this limitation by controlling the dislocation density and thermal stability of a steel alloy produced by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology. We show that by manipulating the alloy’s solidification structure, we can ‘program’ recrystallization upon heat treatment without using mechanical deformation. When employed site-specifically, our strategy enables designing and creating complex microstructure architectures that combine recrystallized and non-recrystallized regions with different microstructural features and properties. We show how this heterogeneity may be conducive to materials with superior performance compared to those with monolithic microstructure. Additive manufacturing of an ultrastrong, deformable Al alloy with nanoscale intermetallics

Abstract: AbstractLight-weight, high-strength, aluminum (Al) alloys have widespread industrial applications. However, most commercially available high-strength Al alloys, like AA 7075, are not suitable for additive manufacturing due to their high susceptibility to solidification cracking. In this work, a custom Al alloy Al92Ti2Fe2Co2Ni2 is fabricated by selective laser melting. Heterogeneous nanoscale medium-entropy intermetallic lamella form in the as-printed Al alloy. Macroscale compression tests reveal a combination of high strength, over 700 MPa, and prominent plastic deformability. Harnessing metastability for grain size control in multiprincipal element alloys during additive manufacturing

Abstract: Controlling microstructure in fusion-based metal additive manufacturing (AM) remains a significant challenge due to the many parameters that directly impact solidification condition. Multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high entropy alloys, offer a vast compositional space to design for microstructural engineering due to their chemical complexity and exceptional properties. Here, we use the FeMnCoCr system as a model platform for exploring alloy design in MPEAs for AM. By exploiting the decreasing stability of the face-centered cubic phase with increasing Mn content, we achieve notable grain refinement and breakdown of epitaxial columnar grain growth. We employ a multifaceted approach encompassing thermodynamic modeling, operando synchrotron X-ray diffraction, multiscale microstructural characterization, and mechanical testing to gain insight into the solidification physics and its ramifications on the resulting microstructure of FeMnCoCr MPEAs.
